findings.description: The bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration block, so objects (including uploaded seed data) are stored unencrypted by default, violating encryption-at-rest requirements.
This bucket stores ledger/financial export data but defines no server_side_encryption_configuration, leaving sensitive financial records unencrypted at rest.
No server_side_encryption_configuration is defined for this bucket, so model artifacts are stored without encryption at rest despite versioning and logging being configured.
The bucket lacks a server_side_encryption_configuration block, leaving operational runbook content (potentially containing sensitive operational/credential details) unencrypted at rest.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block resource is associated with this bucket, so there is no explicit guard preventing future public ACLs or bucket policies from exposing its contents.
No public access block configuration is defined for this financial data bucket, leaving it reliant solely on the current ACL/policy state to remain private.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is configured, so there is no defense-in-depth control against accidental public exposure of proprietary model artifacts.
No public access block is defined, leaving the bucket without an explicit safeguard against future public exposure.
Despite storing audit log data and using an ACL intended for log delivery, no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block resource is configured to explicitly block public access at the bucket level.

This object (vendor-roster.xlsx, likely containing sensitive vendor/PII data) is uploaded without any kms_key_id or server-side encryption parameter, and lands in a bucket that itself has no default encryption configured.
